title: Music, tattoos, and scholars who differ
hookLine: two everyday questions where Muslim scholars genuinely disagree, and what to do with a disagreement
last: MUSHTABIHAT — LEAVE WHAT MAKES YOU DOUBT.

cards: Two questions turn up in almost every Muslim group chat sooner or later. One: is music haram? Usually asked by someone with headphones on.
Two: are tattoos haram? Sometimes asked by someone who already has one, and is quietly wondering whether their prayers count. The internet answers both with total confidence, in both directions.
The honest answer is that scholars have disagreed, carefully, for a very long time. Today: ikhtilaf.

teach.h: IKHTILAF: VIEWS KEPT SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Ikhtilaf means disagreement, and in Islamic law it isn't a scandal. It's a field of study. Scholars working from the same Qur'an and hadith can reach different rulings, and the tradition kept their views side by side.
Day three hundred seven goes deeper. Here are two examples. Music first.
Many classical scholars, across the four Sunni schools, held that musical instruments are not allowed, pointing to a hadith in Bukhari that warns of people who will treat instruments as lawful.
Other scholars questioned that hadith's chain or its meaning: Ibn Hazm in Spain, and, with conditions, al-Ghazali, allowed singing and some instruments when the words and the setting are clean.

Nearly all allow the daff, the frame drum, at weddings, and you met the two girls singing on Eid on day one hundred twenty-seven. Many Muslims today choose voice-only nasheeds as a middle road. Then tattoos.
Most Sunni scholars hold that a permanent tattoo is forbidden, citing a hadith in Bukhari that curses the one who tattoos and the one who is tattooed.
Many Shia jurists see it differently, and allow tattoos whose content is decent.

teach.h: TATTOOS: AN OLD ONE DOESN'T STOP PRAYER.
teach.b: And on the worry that keeps people up at night, there's wide agreement: if you already have one, from before you practiced or before you knew, your wudu and your prayer count.
Many scholars say there's no need to remove it, and nearly all say not if removing it would cause harm. So what do you do with a disagreement?

teach.h: NOT THE EASIEST VIEW. ASK WHY.
teach.b: The tradition's answer: don't grab the easiest view, or the loudest one, and don't sneer at people who follow the other. Ask a teacher you trust, and ask why.

how: On contested questions like music and tattoos, many Muslims follow the view of their school, a local imam or a scholar they trust; some avoid instruments and listen to voice-only nasheeds, others listen to music with clean words.

games.q: a friend says: one scholar online says music is fine, another says it's haram, so I'll just pick the easiest. what does today's lesson suggest?
o: pick the easiest; it doesn't matter.
ask a teacher you trust, and ask why.
games.why: the tradition's way through a disagreement: neither the easiest nor the loudest view, but one you understand, from someone you trust.

practice: Close your eyes if you like, and find the nearest sound: a fan, traffic, a bird, your own breath. Stay with that one sound, then notice the quiet underneath it, the space the sound sits in.
When your mind starts arguing, about music or anything else, come back to the one sound.

wordCard.voice: Ikhtilaf. Disagreement among scholars, worked out carefully from the same sources, and kept side by side rather than erased. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: difference, disagreement; in law, the recorded differences among scholars.

carryVoice: Your line: where scholars differ, ask why. Not the easiest view, not the loudest: one you understand, from someone you trust. Day one hundred forty-eight, in the books.
